You are given an attached CSV file b3_supercon_data.csv: 300 real samples,
column `composition` (element fractions as a compact formula string) and
column `target` (the measured critical temperature Tc (K)).

Propose a composition — a value for each element fraction below, within each
observed range, that MAXIMIZES critical temperature Tc (K) AND stays robust
— its critical temperature Tc (K) must not collapse under a ±5% change in
any single variable (seek a broad optimum, not a sharp peak). Design
variables:
  - O (fraction in [0, 0.697674])
  - Cu (fraction in [0, 0.454545])
  - Ba (fraction in [0, 0.333333])
  - Sr (fraction in [0, 0.285714])
  - Y (fraction in [0, 0.4])
  - Ca (fraction in [0, 0.272727])
  - La (fraction in [0, 0.78])
  - Bi (fraction in [0, 0.521978])
  - Fe (fraction in [0, 0.502513])
  - Nb (fraction in [0, 0.98])
  - C (fraction in [0, 0.972])
  - Pr (fraction in [0, 0.265043])
  - As (fraction in [0, 0.5])
  - B (fraction in [0, 1])
  - Pb (fraction in [0, 0.5])
  - Ce (fraction in [0, 0.28])
  - Mo (fraction in [0, 1])
  - V (fraction in [0, 0.9918])
  - Zn (fraction in [0, 1])

Reason from the training data, then end with your explicit proposal, e.g.

Ca=0.136364, La=0.39, Bi=0.260989, Fe=0.251256, Nb=0.49, C=0.486,

turns.answer_text:
## Reasoning from the data

**1. Where the high‑Tc samples live.** Sorting the 300 samples, everything above ~100 K is a layered cuprate built from only a handful of the design elements:

| Composition | Tc (K) | O | Cu | Ba | Sr | Ca | other |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hg1Ba2Ca2Cu3O8 | 132 | 0.500 | 0.188 | 0.125 | – | 0.125 | Hg |
| Ba2Ca2Cu3O | 126 | 0.125 | 0.375 | 0.250 | – | 0.250 | – |
| Tl0.5Pb0.5Ba1.6Sr0.4Ca2Cu3O | 120 | 0.125 | 0.375 | 0.200 | 0.050 | 0.250 | Tl,Pb |
| Tl0.5Pb0.5Sr2Ca2Cu3Li0.2O | 117 | 0.12 | 0.36 | – | 0.24 | 0.24 | Tl,Pb |
| Bi2Sr2Ca1Cu2O10 | 110 | 0.53 | 0.105 | – | 0.105 | 0.053 | Bi |
| Bi2Sr2Ca2Cu3O | 106 | 0.10 | 0.30 | 0.20 | – | 0.20 | Bi |
| Y1Ba2Cu3O7 (90 K class) | ~90 | 0.54 | 0.23 | 0.15 | – | – | Y |

**2. What drives Tc up.** The consistent signature is **Cu present at a substantial fraction (0.19–0.38), alkaline earths Ba + Ca each ~0.12–0.25, and O anywhere from ~0.1 to ~0.54** (the wide O spread is largely notation, so Tc is *flat* in O over that range — ideal for robustness). Sr can substitute for Ba but the very best members are Ba‑rich; Bi/Pb/Tl are only charge‑reservoir spectators and appear in both 110 K and 26 K samples, so they are not reliable levers.

**3. What kills Tc.** Every sample containing appreciable Fe, As, Nb, Mo, V, B, C, Zn, Ni, Ce, Pr as a *majority* constituent sits below ~55 K (MgB₂ 39 K, Nb₃Sn 18 K, Fe‑pnictides ≤ 56 K, Zn/Ni/V/Mo alloys ≤ 12 K). La and Y are only mildly useful (La₂CuO₄ 35 K, YBCO 90 K) but pull the average down relative to Hg/Tl‑1223‑type ratios, and Pr is a known Tc suppressor. These should be set to **zero** — which also makes them perfectly robust (±5 % of 0 is still 0).

**4. Robustness strategy.** Rather than sitting on any single record point (e.g. the O = 0.5 Hg‑1223 point or the O = 0.125 Ba‑Ca‑Cu‑O point), I place the design in the **centroid of the whole >100 K cluster**: Cu ≈ 0.26, Ca ≈ 0.14, Ba ≈ 0.16, O ≈ 0.42, with a token Sr for the Ba/Sr‑mixed 120 K family. Every one of these values is interior to the high‑Tc band, so a ±5 % perturbation of any single coordinate (e.g. Cu 0.247–0.273, O 0.399–0.441, Ba 0.152–0.168) keeps the point inside the same cluster and cannot fall off a cliff. The fractions also sum to 1.0, keeping the vector physically/statistically in‑distribution (≈ Ba₁.₆Sr₀.₂Ca₁.₄Cu₂.₆O₄.₂, i.e. a Hg/Tl‑1223‑like triple‑CuO₂‑layer stoichiometry).

**Final: O=0.42, Cu=0.26, Ba=0.16, Sr=0.02, Y=0, Ca=0.14, La=0, Bi=0, Fe=0, Nb=0, C=0, Pr=0, As=0, B=0, Pb=0, Ce=0, Mo=0, V=0, Zn=0, Ni=0**
